title: Design a Global Mobile Edge Gateway on QUIC & HTTP/3
tagline: Architect a 20M-connection global HTTP/3 edge gateway using encrypted Connection-ID eBPF routing, 0-RTT anti-replay guards, and UDP GSO/GRO offload.
purpose: Design a multi-PoP QUIC/HTTP/3 edge gateway that survives Wi-Fi-to-5G IP migrations, UDP reflection floods, and rolling deploys with zero dropped streams.

spark.summary: Stateless eBPF load balancers extract encrypted Server-IDs from QUIC Connection IDs to keep mobile connections pinned across IP switches, backed by 3x amplification caps and 0-RTT strike registers.
spark.keyTakeaway: To bound blast radius during partial cluster failures, never hash UDP/443 by 4-tuple IP:Port at L4—embed a cryptographic Server-ID in the Connection ID so eBPF routers survive mobile handoffs statelessly.
spark.byteSummary:
Designing a global edge gateway serving 20M concurrent mobile connections on HTTP/3 over UDP breaks almost every assumption of traditional TCP L4 load balancers. Standard ECMP routers hash the 4-tuple (src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port) to pick a backend QUIC termination worker; the moment a commuter's phone switches from Wi-Fi to 5G—or experiences carrier-grade NAT port rebinding—the 4-tuple hash lands on a different worker pod that lacks the TLS AEAD session keys, instantly killing the connection.

A production QUIC edge gateway solves this by embedding a deterministic Server-ID + Key-Rotation Epoch directly inside the 64-to-128-bit Connection ID (CID) generated by the termination worker (and obfuscated with SipHash/AES so clients cannot infer topology). Stateless eBPF/XDP L4 load balancers inspect the fixed CID offset on every incoming UDP/443 short-header packet and route it to the exact owning worker pod—even across IP changes and BGP Anycast PoP shifts.

To survive internet-scale abuse and edge restarts, the architecture pairs 3x unvalidated-address amplification limits with a distributed 0-RTT anti-replay Bloom/strike register, UDP GSO/GRO kernel batching to halve user-space CPU cost, and graceful GOAWAY + NEW_CONNECTION_ID draining during rolling worker deployments.

learningJourney.title: Sizing 20M Mobile Connections, 2M RPS & Zero-Drop Migrations
learningJourney.purpose: Size connection state, UDP/443 throughput, and sub-50 ms handshake budgets across global Anycast PoPs.

explanation.foundation: Target 20M concurrent mobile QUIC connections across 40 Anycast BGP PoPs (~500K connections/PoP), sustaining 2M RPS and 200K connection migrations/sec during commute peaks.
explanation.core: Each QUIC connection state (TLS keys, stream buffers, BBRv2 pacing state) consumes ~16-24 KB RAM (~8-12 GB per 500K-conn PoP), fitting cleanly across 8-12 edge termination workers per PoP.
explanation.deepDive: Assuming 1,200-byte minimum padded Initial packets, 200K new handshakes/sec require ~2 Gbps of ingress handshake bandwidth per PoP and strict 3x amplification enforcement prior to address validation.

learningJourney.title: Anycast PoPs + eBPF L4 Load Balancing via Embedded CID Server-IDs
learningJourney.purpose: Route UDP/443 packets deterministically by embedded Connection ID Server-ID bits instead of fragile 4-tuple hashes.

explanation.foundation: Standard L4 ECMP hashes `(src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port)`. On Wi-Fi-to-5G migration, `src_ip` and `src_port` change, causing ECMP to misroute packets to a worker without the connection's TLS state.
explanation.core: Workers encode `[Epoch (4b) | Server_ID (20b) | Nonce (40b)]` encrypted with a shared PoP-local AES/SipHash key into every 64-bit CID. The stateless eBPF/XDP L4 balancer decrypts the first 8 bytes of the short header to extract `Server_ID` in <100 ns.
explanation.deepDive: If a BGP route flap shifts a client to a new Anycast PoP mid-connection, the foreign PoP either tunnels the packet over a lightweight GRE/Geneve mesh to the home PoP or issues `RETRY`/stateless reset.

cards.label: Zero Shared Routing Table
cards.detail: Stateless eBPF balancers need no per-connection NAT table—handling 20M flows in constant memory.

cards.label: Topology Privacy
cards.detail: Encrypting Server_ID inside the CID with a rotating PoP key prevents external topology mapping.

cards.label: Migration Immunity
cards.detail: Client IP and NAT port changes leave the CID Server_ID untouched, preserving worker affinity.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Design a Global Mobile Edge Gateway on QUIC & HTTP/3 without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: To bound blast radius during partial cluster failures, never hash UDP/443 by 4-tuple IP:Port at L4—embed a cryptographic Server-ID in the Connection ID so eBPF routers survive mobile handoffs statelessly.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

decisionExercise.prompt: When Design a Global Mobile Edge Gateway on QUIC & HTTP/3 experiences a sudden 5x traffic spike alongside a slow downstream dependency, which engineering choice best protects system stability?

options.label: Increase retry counts and remove client timeouts so every request eventually succeeds.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries multiply load on an already struggling dependency and exhaust worker pools.

options.label: Enforce strict latency budgets, bounded jittered retries, and graceful fallback or load shedding.
options.explanation: Bounding retries and isolating slow paths preserves healthy capacity and keeps tail latency predictable.

learningJourney.title: CID Server-ID Decoder, 0-RTT Strike Gate & Graceful Drain
learningJourney.purpose: Implement stateless CID Server-ID extraction with fallback hashing and replay-safe 0-RTT admission.

explanation.foundation: Every incoming short-header packet must validate CID length, extract the target worker ID safely, and fall back gracefully during rolling drains.
explanation.deepDive: When a worker drains, keep its `Server_ID` mapped in `active_workers` for existing short-header flows while removing it from new-handshake Initial rotation so live connections finish cleanly.

cards.label: Safe Bounds Check
cards.detail: Packets shorter than 8-byte CID fall back cleanly without out-of-bounds reads.

cards.label: Two-Phase Drain
cards.detail: Remove draining workers from Initial-packet rotation first while honoring existing CIDs for 60s.

cards.label: Stateless Reset
cards.detail: Unknown retired CIDs receive a cryptographic Stateless Reset token so clients reconnect fast.

sectionDiagram.summary: Bounds-checked CID decoding and two-phase worker draining preserve live mobile sessions during deploys.

learningJourney.title: UDP GSO/GRO Batching, BBRv2 Pacing & Origin Connection Pooling
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate per-packet syscall bottlenecks and absorb bursty mobile reconnections without saturating origin pools.

explanation.foundation: Without kernel offload, 2M RPS of 1,200B packets triggers millions of `sendmsg` syscalls per second.
explanation.core: Enable `UDP_SEGMENT` (GSO) and `UDP_GRO` on worker sockets, pin one QUIC reactor thread per NIC RSS RX queue (`SO_REUSEPORT` + eBPF), and multiplex decoded HTTP/3 requests onto persistent HTTP/2/gRPC origin pools.
explanation.deepDive: Use BBRv2 pacing in user-space QUIC so 64 KB GSO bursts don't overflow shallow cellular base-station queues.

sectionDiagram.title: UDP GSO/GRO Batching, BBRv2 Pacing & Origin Connection Pooling

cards.label: RSS Core Pinning
cards.detail: Binding one QUIC event loop per NIC RX queue eliminates cross-core packet locks.

cards.label: 64 KB GSO Trains
cards.detail: Passing 50 segments in one sendmsg() closes the CPU gap with kernel TCP.

cards.label: Backend Multiplexing
cards.detail: Edge workers terminate QUIC and reuse warm HTTP/2/gRPC pools to origin services.

sectionDiagram.summary: NIC RSS core pinning, UDP GSO/GRO batching, and BBRv2 pacing keep edge CPU low and origin connections pooled.
sectionDiagram.caption: NIC RSS core pinning, UDP GSO/GRO batching, and BBRv2 pacing keep edge CPU low and origin connections pooled.

learningJourney.title: 3x Amplification Shield, RETRY Tokens & 0-RTT Strike Registers
learningJourney.purpose: Defend UDP/443 ingress against reflection amplification, Initial floods, and 0-RTT replay attacks.

explanation.foundation: UDP port 443 is a prime target for spoofed-IP Initial floods and 0-RTT replay probes.
explanation.core: Under normal load, enforce RFC 9000's 3x unvalidated-byte limit. Under Initial flood (>20K Initials/sec/PoP), switch eBPF/worker ingress to stateless **QUIC RETRY** packets carrying an HMAC-signed address-validation token—costing zero server state.
explanation.deepDive: Run a PoP-local rotating Bloom/strike register (10s window, 2 alternating filters) to block 0-RTT ticket replays with HTTP 425.

sectionDiagram.title: 3x Amplification Shield, RETRY Tokens & 0-RTT Strike Registers

cards.label: Zero-RAM Flood Defense
cards.detail: Stateless RETRY challenges drop spoofed-source floods before allocating TLS or connection state.

cards.label: Dual-Generation Bloom
cards.detail: Alternating 10-second Bloom filters prevent unbounded memory growth while catching all 0-RTT replays.

cards.label: Strict Verb Allowlist
cards.detail: Block non-idempotent verbs in 0-RTT unconditionally at the gateway.

sectionDiagram.summary: Stateless RETRY challenges, 3x amplification caps, and rotating 0-RTT strike filters absorb UDP floods with zero state exhaustion.
sectionDiagram.caption: Stateless RETRY challenges, 3x amplification caps, and rotating 0-RTT strike filters absorb UDP floods with zero state exhaustion.

learningJourney.title: Zero-Drop Worker Deploys via HTTP/3 GOAWAY & Stateless Resets
learningJourney.purpose: Drain 500K-connection PoP workers cleanly during upgrades without breaking in-flight mobile requests.

explanation.foundation: Killing a QUIC worker pod abruptly drops 50K active mobile connections and forces slow timeout-based client retries.
explanation.core: On SIGTERM, the worker stops accepting new Initial CIDs, sends an **HTTP/3 GOAWAY** frame (`last_stream_id`) so clients open new streams on healthy pods, and finishes in-flight streams for up to 60 seconds.
explanation.deepDive: Any packet arriving after shutdown triggers an encrypted **Stateless Reset** (generated from a cluster-wide static reset secret + CID), prompting clients to reconnect immediately instead of waiting 30s for PTO timeouts.

sectionDiagram.title: Zero-Drop Worker Deploys via HTTP/3 GOAWAY & Stateless Resets

cards.label: Client-Visible Drain
cards.detail: HTTP/3 GOAWAY lets clients finish in-flight responses while routing new requests to fresh workers.

cards.label: Shared Reset Secret
cards.detail: Derived HMAC reset tokens let any PoP node abort dead CIDs immediately without holding state.

cards.label: Epoch Rotation
cards.detail: Bump the 4-bit CID epoch on deploy so eBPF never confuses old and new worker IDs.

sectionDiagram.summary: HTTP/3 GOAWAY frames and HMAC-derived Stateless Reset tokens eliminate deploy-time connection stalls.
sectionDiagram.caption: HTTP/3 GOAWAY frames and HMAC-derived Stateless Reset tokens eliminate deploy-time connection stalls.

learningJourney.title: Monitoring QLOG Loss, Anycast Flap Drops & Alt-Svc Circuit Breakers
learningJourney.purpose: Detect ISP UDP throttling, CID misroutes, and 0-RTT replay spikes before mobile p99 degrades.

explanation.foundation: Encrypted QUIC traffic hides packet drops from traditional L4 switch counters.
explanation.core: Sample 1% QLOG traces per PoP, export `quic_cid_misroute_total`, `quic_0rtt_425_total`, `quic_retry_triggered_total`, and `h3_to_h2_fallback_ratio` per ASN.
explanation.deepDive: If an ASN's H3->H2 fallback ratio spikes >15% or BGP Anycast flaps cause >2% CID misroutes, trip an automated edge guardrail that suppresses `Alt-Svc: h3` headers for that region until the path stabilizes.

sectionDiagram.title: Monitoring QLOG Loss, Anycast Flap Drops & Alt-Svc Circuit Breakers

cards.label: Misroute Early Warning
cards.detail: Any spike in unknown-CID Stateless Resets points directly to an eBPF or BGP routing mismatch.

cards.label: Per-ASN Alt-Svc Guard
cards.detail: Suppressing Alt-Svc headers for broken mobile carriers restores instant HTTP/2 loads.

cards.label: Strike-Filter Saturation
cards.detail: Alert if 0-RTT 425 rejections spike, indicating clock skew or active replay probing.

sectionDiagram.summary: QLOG sampling, CID misroute counters, and per-ASN Alt-Svc circuit breakers keep global HTTP/3 edge fleets reliable.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does standard 4-tuple ECMP load balancing break active mobile QUIC connections when a user leaves Wi-Fi for 5G?

options.text: The client's source IP and NAT port change, hashing the packet to a different worker pod that lacks the TLS AEAD session keys.
options.feedback: Correct! Routing by embedded Connection ID Server-ID bits keeps packets hitting the owning worker regardless of IP:Port.

options.text: ECMP routers strip UDP headers from packets above 512 bytes.
options.feedback: ECMP does not strip UDP headers; it hashes the 4-tuple.

options.text: 5G networks block all encrypted packets carrying Connection IDs.
options.feedback: 5G carries standard UDP/443 QUIC traffic normally.

options.text: TLS 1.3 keys are derived from the client's MAC address.
options.feedback: TLS 1.3 session keys are independent of client IP or MAC addresses.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: 4-tuple hashing maps the new 5G IP:Port to a different backend worker unless the L4 balancer routes by the QUIC Connection ID.

knowledgeChecks.question: During a 500K-packet/sec spoofed-IP UDP/443 Initial flood, how should the QUIC edge gateway validate real clients without exhausting worker RAM?

options.text: Allocate full TLS handshake state for every Initial packet and expire after 60 seconds.
options.feedback: Allocating per-packet state under a spoofed flood immediately OOMs the worker.

options.text: Respond with a stateless QUIC RETRY packet containing an HMAC-signed address-validation token, allocating state only after the client echoes it.
options.feedback: Correct! Stateless RETRY proves return-routability with zero server-side memory allocation.

options.text: Send 100 KB of TLS certificates immediately to overwhelm the attacker.
options.feedback: That violates RFC 9000's 3x amplification limit and turns your gateway into a DDoS reflector.
Disabling HTTP/3 degrades all healthy mobile traffic unnecessarily.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Stateless RETRY tokens validate client source IPs using zero worker memory while enforcing the 3x amplification cap.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens if an edge worker is terminated abruptly with SIGKILL instead of sending HTTP/3 GOAWAY and supporting Stateless Resets?

options.text: Clients immediately switch to 0-RTT on the same socket within 1 ms.
options.feedback: Clients don't know the worker died until PTO timeouts expire unless they receive a Stateless Reset.

options.text: In-flight streams fail mid-response and mobile clients stall waiting up to 30s for Probe Timeout (PTO) retries.
options.feedback: Correct! GOAWAY drains active streams cleanly, and Stateless Resets let orphaned CIDs reconnect immediately.

options.text: The eBPF load balancer automatically migrates TLS keys to another pod.
options.feedback: eBPF is stateless and does not hold or migrate user-space TLS session state.

options.text: The kernel TCP stack sends a FIN packet on behalf of the UDP socket.
options.feedback: UDP sockets have no kernel FIN state machine.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Graceful HTTP/3 GOAWAY draining plus HMAC-based Stateless Reset tokens prevent 30-second client hangs during deploys.

prerequisites.title: QUIC & HTTP/3: 0-RTT Handshakes, Stream Multiplexing & Connection Migration
prerequisites.summary: QUIC + HTTP/3 moves multiplexed streaming and TLS 1.3 into user-space over UDP, isolating packet loss per stream and surviving Wi-Fi-to-5G IP changes via Connection IDs.

prerequisites.title: Consistent Hashing & Virtual Nodes
prerequisites.summary: Consistent hashing assigns data keys to servers in a way that limits how many keys move when servers are added or removed. This helps avoid widespread cache misses and sudden load on databases.

prerequisites.title: eBPF & XDP In-Kernel Packet Processing
prerequisites.summary: eBPF runs sandboxed, JIT-compiled bytecode safely inside the Linux kernel, and XDP (eXpress Data Path) hooks directly into the NIC driver RX ring before sk_buff allocation—enabling 20M+ PPS filtering per core.
